title: You and the Puppet: Greg Ashman’s Mind Trick for Helping with Emotional Constancy -constancy/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart revisits his advice that avoiding burnout starts with remembering you are not your job, picturing identity and work performance as two circles that overlap but should not coincide. When identity is rooted in performance, success inflates pride and failure crushes or tempts a teacher to hide. He then brings in Greg Ashman's classroom-management advice to stay calm and assertive, and Ashman's trick of imagining 'the teacher' as a puppet the real self operates. Because students react to the role rather than the person, hurtful remarks land more softly and the teacher can treat a bad lesson as a puzzle rather than a verdict. Stuart frames this as managing one's locus of identity so teacher joy can survive emotional storms.
points: Keeping identity and job performance partly separate, like overlapping circles, protects teachers from pride after success and collapse after failure.
Losing your temper models poor behavior and hands students a gossip-worthy reward, while sticking to observable facts cools the situation.
Ashman's puppet image lets teachers experiment with 'the teacher' role and treat hurtful student remarks as aimed at the role, not the person.
After a rough class, reflecting on what happened like a puzzle builds constancy and sustains teacher joy.
quotes: When your identity as a person is rooted in your performance at work, you’ll end up struggling with all kinds of things. When you succeed, you’ll get puffed up with pride and become insufferable. When you fail, you’ll be smashed to smithereens or you’ll pretend the failure didn’t happen or you’ll start closing your door more so no one else sees.

It helps to think here of two circles: one is your identity, and the other is your performance at work. What you want is for your identity and your work to look like a Venn diagram. You do want some connection between the circles because there’s a goodness in taking ownership of how things go at work, in engaging yourself in what you do.

If you lose your temper, then not only are you modeling poor behavior, to some extent you are also giving students a gossip-worthy reward. Focusing on the facts, the observable behaviors, helps reduce the emotional heat.

I used to imagine that ‘the teacher’ was a puppet under my control, [and that] I could experiment with what the teacher did and see how the students responded. This helps when students inevitably say hurtful things that they don’t really mean. They are reacting to ‘the teacher’ and not to you as an individual

As you prepare for that class that you’re having a hard time with, you can imagine that, come class time, you’re going to have the chance to deploy a lifelike puppet to do your bidding. You’ll have the puppet work to teach the students as best you can. But when things don’t go right for the puppet, picture yourself pondering what happened and working it out — like a puzzle, so to speak.

What Greg’s mind trick helps us do is manage what psychologists call our locus of identity. It helps us do what we want to do — to stoke the fires of teacher joy while also warding against the storms of emotion. You and I aren’t meant to have our sense of self be dependent on something as elusive as our daily performance in the classroom.
